k.t01-apar-0: EXPLANATORY BOOKLET FOR the Delmas Auxiliary Charts ❦ FIRST SERIES
k.t01-apar-1: CHART No. 1 The School. — The Secondary School. — The Classroom.
k.t01-01-1: 1. — This chart shows a classroom in a secondary school. In this classroom there are eight tables  and eight benches . Three pupils sit on each bench. The teacher  sits on a chair  at his desk .
k.t01-02-1: 2. — To the left of the desk stands a glass-fronted cabinet . To the right is the blackboard  with the cloth  and the chalk .
k.t01-02-2: Above the desk hang wall charts (, , ) and a map .
k.t01-03-1: 3. — Not all the pupils are in their seats . John  is standing at the board; he is holding the cloth and wiping off the geometrical figures.
k.t01-03-2: Peter is near the desk; he is collecting the written exercises  and bringing them to the teacher.
k.t01-04-1: 4. — This teacher is the teacher of modern languages. He teaches the pupils to speak, read and write foreign languages (German, English, Spanish, Italian, Russian or French).
k.t01-05-1: 5. — The classroom is very large and very bright. At the far end there is a wide window with two transoms  and a glazed door to air it and light it.
k.t01-05-2: This classroom is not cold. In the middle, to heat it, there is a very good stove  with its pipe .
k.t01-05-3: Coat hooks  are fixed to the partition; the pupils’ hats and coats hang from them.
k.t01-06-1: 6. — The clock  says five past nine.
k.t01-06-2: Break  has just ended and the lesson is starting again. Break is held in the yard . We can see a few pupils playing. An assistant master  is supervising them.
k.t01-07-1: 7. — In the yard we can also see various other people: the inspector , the headmaster  and the deputy head .
k.t01-07-2: The inspector inspects the schools, the headmaster runs the school, the deputy head oversees the pupils’ work.
k.t01-07-3: The fourth figure is the caretaker . He is carrying a register under his arm to record the absentees.
k.t01-08-1: 8. — At the far end of the yard are the gymnastic apparatus  and the workshop for handicrafts .
k.t01-08-2: To the right of the chart we can just make out the classrooms for music and drawing.
k.t01-09-1: 9. — The pupils on the first bench to the right of the desk are Henry , Stephen and Charles.
k.t01-09-2: Henry is very attentive and hard-working; he is listening to the teacher. On his table he has an exercise book , a book , a dictionary  and a pencil case . His book has many pages; each chapter contains several paragraphs and each line many words.
k.t01-09-4: His neighbour Stephen  is keen. He is writing down in his exercise book the lesson set for next time. He has fine handwriting. His book is closed. We can see only the cover . Beside him lies his pair of compasses .
k.t01-09-5: Charles  is holding his book in his hand; he is opening it to go over his lesson again. Like every pupil, he has an inkwell  in front of him. He is obedient.
k.t01-10-1: 10. — At the next table are Louis, Anthony and Paul. Louis is reciting his lesson  and answering the teacher’s questions. Anthony  is very inattentive; sometimes the teacher even punishes him. Paul  is a good friend, pleasant and obliging. He is very attentive.
k.t01-11-1: 11. — Behind Henry sits George . He is not a bad lad, but he is talkative, inattentive and fidgety. His frivolity and disobedience cause disruption during the lesson, and he often deserves a stern warning. His rough book  is dirty, he covers it with ink blots from his pen , which is why he always uses his eraser ; his satchel  is torn, for he is very careless. Why does he bring his pencil holder  to the modern languages classroom?
k.t01-11-2: His neighbour Edmund  does not like him. He is admittedly a little lazy, but he is quiet and still. He does not chatter; only, instead of listening, he prefers to read the stories in his reader.
k.t01-11-3: The third pupil on this bench is Ludovic . He is diligent. He is writing on a white sheet of paper. In front of him he has laid his blotting paper .
k.t01-12-1: 12. — The pupils on the second bench, to the teacher’s left, are very young. The first, little Emil, cannot write well yet; he brings his slate , his slate pencil and his sponge .
k.t01-12-2: Next to him are Augustus and Bernard . The latter works well, but his appearance is very untidy.
k.t01-13-1: 13. — Behind them sit three idlers. Albert does not learn his lessons. James  is asleep instead of listening. His idleness earns him reprimands and even punishments. Lastly Christian  is far too flippant. He behaves badly and makes no effort to mend his ways.
k.t01-14-1: 14. — Their neighbours, by contrast, are well behaved. Ernest  likes order and regularity; he always uses his ruler  and his pencil . He is a day pupil.
k.t01-14-2: Francis  is a boarder; he wears the uniform, and eats and sleeps at the school. He is a good friend.
k.t01-14-3: Maurice is sharpening his pencil with his penknife ; he is very careful.
k.t01-14-4: He brings all his books, his grammar , his notebook , and even a writing pad . His school bag  is on the floor behind him.
k.t01-14-5: The two tables at the back of the classroom are taken by good pupils .
k.t01-15-1: 15. — In the drawing room there are handsome models hung on the wall and a lamp  with a shade, hanging from the ceiling. The teacher  is very patient; he corrects the pupils’ drawings  and teaches them to draw a bust  from life.
k.t01-16-1: 16. — The music room looks very interesting. There one learns to read music, to sing the scale notes  written on the stave (do, re, mi, fa, sol, la, si = C. D. E. F. G. A. B.), to know the clefs and to sing charming melodies. The scores are placed on the music stand . One of the pupils is playing the piano  and the music teacher  is beating time .
k.t01-17-1: 17. — We can just see a corner of the workshop for handicrafts , where the children may learn to plane wood and file iron. Not every school has one.
k.t01-18-1: 18. — The mathematics teacher teaches the pupils geometry, arithmetic, calculation and the metric system. On the chart we can see the main geometrical figures: a circle (), a square (), a triangle (), a line ().
k.t01-18-2: We can also see a sum; it is not an addition, nor a subtraction, nor a multiplication: it is a division ().
k.t01-19-1: 19. — On the metric system chart we can see: a metre (), a balance () and its weights, a litre (), a decalitre (), a decilitre and a cubic metre ().
k.t01-19-2: The pupils also study natural science  — zoology (), botany (), geology () — and history .
k.t01-19-3: In the cabinet are the instruments for physics  and for chemistry .
k.t01-19-4: On top of the cabinet are: a sphere , a cone and a globe .
k.t01-19-5: Above the charts hangs a map showing the five parts of the world: Europe (), Asia (), Africa (), America () and Oceania (), and the two great oceans, the Pacific () and the Atlantic ().
k.t02-apar-1: CHART No. 2 The Human Body. — Break. Games.
k.t02-tit-0: The Human Body. (A simple natural science lesson.)
k.t02-01-1: 1. — The main parts of the human body are: the head, the trunk and the limbs.
k.t02-02-1: 2. — The head has two parts: the skull, which holds the brain and is covered by the hair, and the face.
k.t02-03-1: 3. — In our drawing we can see neither the skull nor the brain; but we can see the important parts of the face very clearly.
k.t02-04-1: 4. — Here first is the forehead, which speaks of a powerful intellect and a mind always at work. The temples are very open. The eye is lively and wide open. A thick eyebrow and long eyelashes shield it.
k.t02-05-1: 5. — Here too are the nose and the nostrils. The nose serves us for smelling and for breathing. On either side of the nose are the cheeks, and further out the ears. The lower part of the face consists of the mouth and the chin.
k.t02-06-1: 6. — We cannot see them very well, for the moustache and the beard hide them from us. But we know that the mouth has the two lips, the upper jaw and the lower jaw with their teeth, and the tongue. With the mouth we speak and eat. With the tongue we taste our food.
k.t02-07-1: 7. — The eye, the ear, the nose and the mouth are, together with the fingers, the organs of the five senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch.
k.t02-08-1: 8. — The head is therefore one of the most interesting parts of the human body.
k.t02-09-1: 9. — The neck joins the head to the trunk. It includes the throat and the nape.
k.t02-10-1: 10. — The trunk also holds many essential organs. In the chest are the lungs, with which we breathe, and the heart, which is the centre of life. When the heart stops beating, the living creature dies.
k.t02-12-1: 12. — The other parts of the trunk are the side, the back, the shoulders and the abdomen (belly). We lie on our side or on our back to sleep, and we carry loads on our shoulder.
k.t02-13-1: 13. — In the abdomen are the stomach and the intestines. They serve us to digest our food.
k.t02-14-1: 14. — We have four limbs: two arms and two legs. With our arms we take, hold, lift and gather up objects; with our legs we stand, walk and run.
k.t02-15-1: 15. — The shoulder joins the arm to the body. A very sturdy muscle, the biceps, moves the arm, which the elbow joins to the forearm. The wrist forms the joint of the hand, which ends in the fingers and the nails. On the hand we can make out a vein (and an artery) in which the blood flows.
k.t02-16-1: 16. — The parts of the leg are: the thigh, the knee and the back of the knee, the calf, whose flesh is covered by the skin, the ankle and the foot. The bones of the leg are very thick and very strong. At the end of the foot are the toes. The other parts are the sole and the heel.
k.t02-17-1: 17. — Such is the almost complete description of the human body.
k.t02-17-2: Note. — With the help of the phrase “my ... hurts (my head, and so on)”, the teacher will be able to go over this whole vocabulary again from the point of view of good or bad bodily health.
k.t02-tit-4: Gymnastics. (Told by one of the pupils.)
k.t02-18-1: 18. — To be supple, nimble and healthy, we must exercise our legs and our arms. That is why we play games and do gymnastics.
k.t02-19-1: 19. — During the week these two exercises take place in the school yard (see chart No. 1). But on Thursdays and Sundays we go out to a large lawn, where we have room to run and enjoy ourselves.
k.t02-20-1: 20. — Our masters and our parents sometimes come with us; but it is the gymnastics teacher  who directs the exercises.
k.t02-21-1: 21. — On the lawn, to the left of the entrance, stands the gymnastic apparatus : we climb the ladder , we swing upside down on the rings  and on the trapeze , we haul ourselves up hand over hand to the top of the rope ladder  or of the knotted rope .
k.t02-22-1: 22. — Meanwhile our friends are vaulting over the wooden horse  or the parallel bars . Others are boxing  or fencing  with a mask and a foil. Others, finally, are lifting dumbbells .
k.t02-23-1: 23. — Around the gymnasts, boys and girls are playing various games. The girls are amusing themselves with their hoop ; they skip , or invite their brothers and cousins to a game of croquet . They are delighted to knock away their opponent’s ball with their wooden mallet, just as he thinks he will pass easily through the hoop!
k.t02-24-1: 24. — The boys prefer more strenuous games. They gladly play skittles , which they knock down neatly with the ball . Nor do they scorn the spinning top  and cup-and-ball , or even toad in the hole . But their favourite games are marbles  and fives , for the wall of the greenhouse  is just right for bouncing the light ball off.
k.t02-25-1: 25. — Little John, up on his stilts , is very skilful and keeps his balance very well. Near him, a few friends are playing hide-and-seek  in that greenhouse and behind the hedge. Others prefer hot cockles  or shuttlecock , which flits from one racket to the other.
k.t02-26-1: 26. — In the middle of the lawn there are two trees. At the foot of one of them, seven or eight boys have got up a game of shoulder-leap  . This game is not known in every country; but everyone knows what leapfrog is, which the children are not playing just now.
k.t02-tit-6: Games in the open air.
k.t02-27-1: 27. — Blind man’s buff  is also great fun; girls and boys take turns to put the blindfold over their eyes and catch the clumsy ones who let themselves be caught.
k.t02-28-1: 28. — In the middle of the lawn, here is a very French game, though a somewhat rough one: it is the bear , far noisier than the peaceful game of the kite  or even than the English game of tennis .
k.t02-29-1: 29. — That last sport is the delight of the older pupils. Our teachers themselves take it up willingly. It calls for great skill and agility, and I like it very much. I leave the swing  to the girls.
k.t02-30-1: 30. — Nor do I care for another English game that could well turn dangerous.
k.t02-30-1b: I mean football , which is my elder brother’s joy. I prefer our old game of prisoner’s base , quite as healthy and much less brutal.
k.t02-tit-7: Cycling and ball games.
k.t02-31-1: 31. — I am also glad to ride round the lawn on a bicycle .
k.t02-32-1: 32. — Next year I shall learn to ride . A horse is such a fine sight when it steps or trots gracefully, and clears the obstacles at a gallop!
k.t02-33-1: 33. — In summer we learn to swim . We dive and bathe with delight in the clear, cool water of the river. Sometimes, at the end, we send up a paper balloon , which rises majestically into the air as soon as it is filled with hot air.
k.t02-34-1: 34. — There are many other games as well, but I would never come to the end of listing them, and one can see from this short account that Thursdays on our fine lawn are anything but dull.
k.t02-34-2: N.B. — The teacher will easily fill out this chapter by describing each of the more important games in greater detail.
k.t03-apar-1: CHART No. 3 Childhood and Youth.
k.t03-apar-2: (Charts 3 and 4 are arranged so as to present, in four family scenes, the essential vocabulary of the weather, age, the family, clothing and health.)
k.t03-tit-2: A christening in the village.
k.t03-c1-01-1: 1. — We are in spring, in the month of March, April or May, on a day of the week — Monday, Tuesday or Wednesday. It is ten o’clock in the morning.
k.t03-c1-02-1: 2. — The weather is fine, the air clear. The sun is shining. A few small clouds  are rising in the blue sky .
k.t03-c1-03-1: 3. — The trees have hardly any leaves. The slender poplars  and the tall plane tree  still bear nothing but buds.
k.t03-c1-04-1: 4. — The swallows  are back, and they wheel with joyful cries around the spire  of the bell tower  that crowns the village church .
k.t03-c1-05-1: 5. — Very plain is this church with its great doorway  and its big clock . The small hand  is on the figure X: it marks the hours. The big one  is on XII (noon); it marks the minutes.
k.t03-c1-06-1: 6. — In the tower the bells  are ringing gaily. At the top of the roof stands a small stone cross .
k.t03-c1-07-1: 7. — The church has not only a great doorway , it also has a small side door. Through this door the parish priest , in his cassock, comes out of the vestry  and makes his way to the presbytery .
k.t03-c1-08-1: 8. — Near him, here is the milkwoman  with her donkey . She is coming back from town, where she has taken her good milk for the children.
k.t03-c1-09-1: 9. — Master Aliboron (the donkey) is quite pleased with this morning run. He breathes in with delight the air scented by the blossom  that covers the fruit trees  of the neighbouring orchard. All pink and white are those peach trees  and apricot trees , and they promise a fine crop.
k.t03-c1-10-1: 10. — Meanwhile the little bees  from the hive  go there to gather their sweet honey, humming as they work.
k.t03-c1-11-1: 11. — But what is happening? Here come the village children, running up and scattering the frightened geese . It is the procession leaving the church after the christening of the notary’s son.
k.t03-c1-12-1: 12. — Little James, in his cradle , wakes at the joyful pealing of the bells, and his sister Madeleine, who wants to see the procession too, asks her mother to come and comb her hair and dress her on the doorstep.
k.t03-c1-13-1: 13. — Her mother agrees. She puts on her headscarf , her bodice  and her apron , and comes and sits on a little chair in front of the door. Madeleine has only her petticoat  and her bodice .
k.t03-c1-14-1: 14. — How happy she is! She forgets her favourite flowers, her carnations , where the butterflies  settle, her tulips , her lilies of the valley  in their pots  on the wall , and her roses  that make so fine a hedge. She is gazing at the rich clothes of the ladies in the procession.
k.t03-c1-15-1: 15. — The village boys pay little attention to the clothes. They rush forward and jostle one another to get sweets  or coins . One of them is crying .
k.t03-c1-16-1: 16. — Another has trodden on the paw of the dog , which runs off yelping and puts to flight the hen  and her chicks .
k.t03-c1-17-1: 17. — At the head of the procession walks the nurse . She has a fine bonnet  with long ribbons. She is carrying the newborn baby , all dressed in lace .
k.t03-c1-18-1: 18. — Behind the nurse come the godfather  and the godmother . They are handing out the sweets and the coins. The godfather has gloves  and a top hat . The godmother is holding a fine bouquet  in her hand.
k.t03-c1-19-1: 19. — Behind them we can see the child’s uncle  and aunt . The aunt has an elegant hat , the uncle a black frock coat  and a white waistcoat. Next come the cousin  and his cousin . The latter is holding by the hand the newborn baby’s sister , little Bertha.
k.t03-c1-20-1: 20. — Bertha’s other brother  walks behind. He is giving his hand to a relative . The family’s friends  come after them.
k.t03-c1-21-1: 21. — Near the procession, here is a beggar  leaning on his crutch . He is asking for alms.
k.t03-c1-22-1: 22. — On the other side is a very polite  little boy. He raises his cap and wishes “good morning” to the people he knows.
k.t03-c1-23-1: 23. — The villagers have come out of their houses to watch the christening procession go by. We can see a countryman  with his cotton cap and beside him a countrywoman . Then an old woman  leaning on her stick . Lastly the miller  with his broad felt hat , and a young countrywoman in clogs  teaching her baby to walk.
k.t03-c1-24-1: 24. — It is a very lively scene.
k.t03-tit-10: Water sports and regatta.
k.t03-c2-01-1: 1. — Summer has come. The blazing sun of the month of June (July or August) tempts the young people to bathe and to go boating.
k.t03-c2-02-1: 2. — On the right bank of the river, the oarsmen are undressing to take part in the water sports and the regatta.
k.t03-c2-03-1: 3. — One of them is taking off his shoes ; he is unlacing (unbuttoning) them. His two friends are ready already. They now have nothing on but their jersey  and bathing trunks . They are chatting as they wait for their friends. They are talking about the fair and the festival being held on the other bank.
k.t03-c2-04-1: 4. — On the ground near them lie their friends’ clothes: a pair of boots , shoes , socks , felt  and straw  hats and a tie .
k.t03-c2-05-1: 5. — One of the young men has carefully folded his jacket . He is laying it on a towel, in which his neighbour will shortly wrap up both their suits.
k.t03-c2-06-1: 6. — A sixth boy is behindhand. He still has his cap  on his head. He has taken off neither his shirt , nor his collar , nor his cuffs . He is holding his waistcoat  in his hand and still has his trousers  and braces  on. He will certainly not be ready for the next race.
k.t03-c2-07-1: 7. — Near the young men, a path lined with thistles  leads down to the riverside, where old James is getting ready, among the reeds , the fireworks  that will be set off in the evening.
k.t03-c2-08-1: 8. — On the river, a few ladies sheltering under their parasols are out in a rowing boat . They are following the race, which is very exciting. In each skiff , four rowers  are pulling with all their strength, while the coxswain  holds the rudder  and steers the fragile craft. The oars  strike the water in time, and the light boats race along at a dizzying speed.
k.t03-c2-09-1: 9. — A few young men are competing, near the pier of the bridge, for the prize of the greasy pole . One of them is edging carefully along the springy, slippery pole to reach the little flag  fixed at the end. His luckless rival  has fallen into the water. He is swimming back to shore.
k.t03-c2-10-1: 10. — Older lads are water-jousting  near the quay . A large crowd  is watching all these games, leaning on the parapet of the bridge  and packed along the bank. A few onlookers, though, are turning round to follow the game of the climbing pole , or to admire the mayoral procession on its way to the prize-giving.
k.t03-c2-11-1: 11. — First, here are a few urchins  running ahead of the bandsmen ; then come the mayor , his deputies and the town council of the little town. Last of all march the firemen .
k.t03-c2-12-1: 12. — There is a great crowd on the fairground . People come to see the various booths: the wooden horses , the circus , where the performance has already begun; the public dance , where the young men and women of the town are enjoying the pleasure of dancing.
k.t03-c2-13-1: 13. — At the far end we can see the arena , where the brave Spanish matador fights the furious bull ; then the switchback  and the shooting gallery , where people practise handling firearms and shooting at the target.
k.t03-c2-14-1: 14. — Close by, here is the fairground theatre , where comedy and drama are performed. Very near it stands the booth of the giant  and the dwarf. The height of the first is two metres fifteen; the second is barely as tall as a child.
k.t03-c2-15-1: 15. — Lastly, here is the great menagerie  with its wild animals, its tiger  with its powerful claws, its lion  with its thick mane, its two giraffes  and its elephant , which uses its trunk so cleverly.
k.t03-c2-16-1: 16. — The tamer  who trains these animals is standing at the door of the booth.
k.t04-apar-1: CHART No. 4 Middle Age and Old Age.
k.t04-tit-1: First scene. The Wedding Breakfast.
k.t04-c1-01-1: 1. — The young people have grown up. One of them, John, is getting married. We are at the wedding breakfast, which brings the families of the bride and groom together around the same table.
k.t04-c1-02-1: 2. — We are in autumn, in the month of September. The cold wind of October and November has not yet stripped the countryside of its green leaves. The evening air is mild and fragrant; so dinner is being served under the veranda  that opens on to the garden.
k.t04-c1-03-1: 3. — In the distance, on the hill , stands the home of John’s parents, an elegant country house  hidden in the greenery; fine vineyards, which yield an excellent wine, cover the slope of the hillside. The winegrower tends and cares for them.
k.t04-c1-04-1: 4. — Above the vines, a covey of partridges  goes by, startled by the approach of the gamekeeper . He, with his gun under his arm and his game bag slung over his shoulder, is beating the bushes  with his dog . He watches over the estate and keeps poachers from destroying the game.
k.t04-c1-05-1: 5. — Outside the veranda climbs a trained vine, from which hang heavy bunches of grapes .
k.t04-c1-06-1: 6. — The fine autumn flowers that decorate the table  are chrysanthemums ; the bride’s father  has put one in the buttonhole of his tailcoat.
k.t04-c1-07-1: 7. — The meal is drawing to a close. The servant  is beginning to bring in the dessert dishes and will soon clear away the various parts of the place settings — spoons , forks , knives , serving dishes  — that are no longer needed.
k.t04-c1-08-1: 8. — Everyone looks cheerful, and the smile with which the groom’s mother  watches her children shows how happy she is.
k.t04-c1-09-1: 9. — This marriage unites two wealthy families of the district. John, the husband , is the son of a great landowner, and he becomes the son-in-law of a successful manufacturer.
k.t04-c1-10-1: 10. — The couple are young, and yet they have been engaged for a long time. The young wife , Martha, looks charming in her white dress trimmed with orange blossom.
k.t04-c1-11-1: 11. — Her father-in-law  is delighted to have so kind a daughter-in-law, and John’s mother-in-law  smiles to see her daughter looking so lovely.
k.t04-c1-12-1: 12. — At the end of the table sit the other guests : relatives, friends, cousins. A head waiter , with his napkin over his arm, is attending to them briskly.
k.t04-c1-13-1: 13. — On the right-hand side of the table, here is a young lady , a friend of the bride, then the bride’s brother, who is her best man . He is chatting with his bridesmaid , the groom’s sister, who by this marriage becomes Martha’s sister-in-law. She is a charming young woman. She has beautiful jewellery, a pearl necklace and a gold bracelet.
k.t04-c1-14-1: 14. — Near them, the gentleman standing and raising his glass is a friend  of the family. He is one of the groom’s witnesses. He is proposing a toast, drinking to the health of the newly-weds and wishing them long happiness. He is in formal dress: tailcoat and patent leather shoes . He is escorting the grandmother , who is a widow.
k.t04-c1-15-1: 15. — The young man in the tailcoat , with the thin black moustache, is John’s brother-in-law . He is a distinguished engineer. He is sitting next to a very elegant young lady , Martha’s elder sister and the mother of the sweet little girl who is coming, on her cousin’s arm, to offer a flower and wish her good evening. This lady has very fine earrings and an elegant hairstyle.
k.t04-c1-16-1: 16. — The little cousin, who looks so odd in his smock  and his baggy breeches , is much to be pitied. He is an orphan . He lost his father and his mother when he was very young. His uncle is his guardian , and stayed single in order to bring the poor child up. He is a kind man. He is rather bald and very short-sighted; he wears pince-nez.
k.t04-c1-17-1: 17. — Behind the guests, on a table covered with a tablecloth, the dessert  is laid out. In a large bowl, here is fruit: peaches , pears , apples , apricots  and grapes . Beside them, pineapples , a fine cake , bottles of liqueur  and champagne , and stacks of clean plates  as well.
k.t04-c1-18-1: 18. — The wine waiter  is uncorking a bottle  of old wine with a corkscrew . The cork  seems very hard to draw. This wine waiter has a napkin  over his arm.
k.t04-c1-19-1: 19. — After dinner the gentlemen will move on to the smoking room, and the ladies will go and get ready for the ball.
k.t04-tit-6: Second scene. Grandfather’s Birthday.
k.t04-c2-01-1: 1. — Ten years have passed. John’s parents have grown old, and they dearly love their three grandchildren, two grandsons  and a granddaughter . As today is grandfather’s birthday, the children have come to wish him many happy returns.
k.t04-c2-02-1: 2. — Little Peter is still very young; he is only three. He sees the cat  coming towards him. He wants to stroke its beautiful silky fur and its long tail; it does not occur to him that, under those graceful paws, there are nasty sharp claws that may well scratch him.
k.t04-c2-03-1: 3. — His sister Gabrielle, who is holding his hand, is much more serious, and Marcel, with his big overcoat  and leather belt , looks quite the little man, in spite of the short breeches that leave his stockings  showing.
k.t04-c2-04-1: 4. — Their father has put on his thick winter overcoat  with its fur collar , and in his pocket  he has a scarf. His wife has her felt hat trimmed with feathers , her jacket , her fur boa  and her muff .
k.t04-c2-05-1: 5. — It is very cold, for winter is here. The snow  has been falling all day and the roofs of the houses are quite white. With night the cold grows sharper still. In the sky, the moon  and the stars  shine and pierce the darkness.
k.t04-c2-06-1: 6. — The poor blind man  crossing the square in front of the chemist’s shop , led by his poodle , is very unfortunate. Justine, the maid , is bringing from the kitchen a bowl  of very hot herbal tea, generously sweetened.
k.t04-c2-07-1: 7. — Grandmother , who wants to fetch her spectacles  from the table so as to read the prescription  the doctor  has just written, is getting up out of her armchair, leaning on her stick .
k.t04-c2-08-1: 8. — She often suffers from small ailments, dizzy spells, colds and toothache; her legs are weak and her eyes are no longer very good. All the same, she is glad to tease her old doctor, who always wants to prescribe her a draught . Today she is very happy to have her young family around her.
k.t04-c2-09-1: 9. — It is snug in the well-shut room. In the marble fireplace  a splendid fire  is blazing, and one feels happy in the soft light of the lamp  that has just been lit.
k.t04-c2-10-1: 10. — Even grandfather  has forgotten that he has been ill, that his rheumatism keeps him fixed in his armchair , and that only yesterday he had a fever and fainting fits. He no longer remembers that last winter he had pneumonia, and that a harsh, painful cough made him suffer a great deal.
k.t04-c2-10-2: And yet he recovered only with difficulty. He is somewhat better now. But his leg, which he rests on a cushion  laid on a small stool , still hurts him too.
k.t04-c2-11-1: 11. — When he is carefully wrapped in his warm dressing gown  with its big mother-of-pearl buttons , and when he has beside him, to read him the paper, the little orphan girl  in her white bonnet, her blue dress  and cape , he does not complain.
k.t04-c2-12-1: 12. — Every year, when the calendar  brings round the date of the first of December again, he waits impatiently for his grandchildren, for he knows they will not forget that important date.
k.t04-c2-13-1: 13. — He remembers with feeling the far-off days when he used to go himself to wish many happy returns to the glorious imperial marshal, whose portrait  hangs on the wall, and who is the children’s great-grandfather.
k.t05-apar-1: CHART No. 5 The House and how it is built.
k.t05-01-1: John. — Uncle, I should very much like to know how a house is built.
k.t05-01-2: The Uncle <button class="lupo" data-g="t05-apar-1" data-c="0.244484,0.692031,0.008246,0.010451" data-n="80" title="" aria-expanded="false"><sup>(80)</sup></button>. — That is easy enough, my boy; come with me and I will show you the one Mr Bernard <button class="lupo" data-g="t05-apar-1" data-c="0.2115,0.682887,0.010252,0.010124" data-n="79" title="" aria-expanded="false"><sup>(79)</sup></button> is having built and that I am going to live in.
k.t05-01-3: John. — And who drew the plan  of this house?
k.t05-01-4: The Uncle. — The architect ; he produced a very clear drawing, it was approved, and the building contractor  began the work.
k.t05-01-5: John. — And who is the contractor?
k.t05-01-6: The Uncle. — Mr White, the father of your friend James. He directs the workmen together with Mr Roux, the architect.
k.t05-01-7: Well now! Here comes Mr White at just the right moment with his rule , and Mr Roux with his plan.
k.t05-01-8: Good morning, gentlemen. How are you?
k.t05-01-9: Mr Roux. — Very well, thank you. Good morning, John; how the boy has grown!
k.t05-01-10: The Uncle. — Indeed he has, he is quite the little man. He is very serious; everything he sees has to be explained to him. Today he would like to know how a house is built.
k.t05-01-11: Mr White. — Come along with me, then, my young friend, and I will explain it to you at once, for I am very fond of children who want to learn.
k.t05-01-12: You see that workman with a shovel  in his hand: he is a navvy . He is digging a trench  to lay the water pipe. He also dug out the ground where the house stands, so that the bricklayer could put up the four walls. The part of those walls that is in the ground is called the foundations . The space enclosed by the foundations forms the cellar . This cellar has a small window called an air vent , a door  and a stairway.
k.t05-01-13: The bricklayer  went on raising the walls, leaving openings for the doors  and the windows .
k.t05-01-14: John. — But I cannot see him, this bricklayer!
k.t05-01-15: Mr White. — He has finished working on the house now. He is over by the stable , up on his scaffolding , building the wall of the wash house .
k.t05-01-16: He has a trowel, a trough and a plumb line . But you will not remember those names.
k.t05-01-17: John. — Oh yes I shall, for I am going to ask my uncle for a little trowel and a trough, and I shall make a plumb line myself with a piece of string.
k.t05-01-18: The Uncle. — Ah, very good. But tell me, John, what do you need to build a house?
k.t05-01-19: John. — You need dressed stone  and mortar .
k.t05-01-20: The Uncle. — Just so. Look at that man in the big hat, on his cart . He is a carter . Every day he brings blocks of stone  here. He unloads his cart in the yard, and the stonecutters  dress the blocks and saw them with their stone saw . A labourer  carries them to the bricklayer, who sets them in place.
k.t05-01-21: Meanwhile the mortar mixer  is preparing the mortar. He needs sand , lime  and water . The lime is beside him in a sack ; a bricklayer’s mate  brings him the sand in a wheelbarrow , and the apprentice  is at the pump . He is filling a bucket . The mortar will soon be ready. The hod carrier  takes it and carries it up the ladder to the scaffolding, where a bricklayer is finishing that side of the house.
k.t05-01-22: And now, what do you call the workman who makes the roof ?
k.t05-01-23: John. — He is the roofer .
k.t05-tit-4: The roof of the house.
k.t05-01-24: Mr White. — Yes, but first comes the carpenter .
k.t05-01-25: The carpenter makes the roof frame . He joins the beams  with pegs . Those workmen up there, in their wide velvet breeches, are carpenters. One is holding a small beam and the other is cutting a peg with his axe . The one near the chimney  is the roofer. He nails laths on to the joists , and slates  on to the laths. Sometimes he lays tiles.
k.t05-01-26: The roof of the stable is tiled , that of the house is slated , and that of the veranda is of zinc .
k.t05-01-27: John. — Does the roofer make the zinc roofs as well?
k.t05-01-28: Mr White. — No, that is the zinc worker  or the plumber, the one setting a dormer window  into the roof of the house. He also lays the roof gutters  and the downpipes . He solders the zinc and the tinplate. It was he who fixed the lightning conductor  and the weathervane  on the gable .
k.t05-01-29: John. — Is the house finished, then?
k.t05-01-30: Mr White. — Not quite. The plasterer  builds with bricks  the partitions that divide it into the different rooms. He coats the ceilings  and the walls with plaster . Just now he is working on the ceiling of the veranda . Like the bricklayer, he has a trowel  and a trough .
k.t05-01-31: Then the joiner makes the doors, the windows, the wooden floors  and the shutters .
k.t05-01-32: Just now he is working in the yard at his workbench . He has a saw  to cut the wood , a plane , a holdfast , a chisel , a pair of compasses  and a wooden mallet .
k.t05-01-33: John. — Oh, but being a joiner is even more fun than being a bricklayer. Uncle, will you buy me a workbench, a saw and a plane? I am going to make a kennel for Medor.
k.t05-01-35: John. — How glad I am! And who is that man standing near the front door?
k.t05-01-36: Mr White. — He is a painter . He is standing on his ladder with a pot of paint  and his brush . He is coating the wood of the front door so that it will last longer.
k.t05-01-37: He is also the one who hangs the wallpaper in the rooms.
k.t05-01-38: The upholsterer  on a ladder , out on the balcony , is putting up a blind .
k.t05-01-39: The workman standing by the big window is the glazier . He fixes the panes  with putty . That other workman, kneeling by the cellar door, is a locksmith . He is fitting a lock . His file  is beside him.
k.t05-01-40: John. — Is the man striking a piece of iron with his hammer  a locksmith too?
k.t05-01-41: Mr White. — More precisely, he is a blacksmith . He is forging ironwork  for the electrician , who is on the roof of the coach house . He has a forge , an anvil  and a pair of tongs .
k.t05-01-42: The electrician is fixing the copper wire  of the telephone.
k.t05-01-43: The Uncle. — At the far end of the yard , near the railings  and the carriage gate , you can see the gardener . He is getting the little garden  ready. He has dug the soil over with his spade , he is sowing seed and raking with the rake . Then, with his watering can , he will water the flower beds  and the plants will grow.
k.t05-01-44: The groom , who has just tended the horse and fed it, is cleaning the carriage  with a sponge, a hand pump  and a bucket of water. Then he will put it away in the coach house and shut the door with the heavy bolt .
k.t05-01-45: There, you are satisfied now, I hope; you have had explanations enough.
k.t05-01-46: John. — Yes, uncle, but I should like to see the inside of the house.
k.t05-01-47: The Uncle. — That will be for tomorrow. Mr Roux will explain the plan to you and tell you the name of each room.
k.t05-tit-8: The layout of the house.
k.t05-01-48: The Architect. — Come, John, I am going to take you round the different parts of the house.
k.t05-01-49: Let us go into the ground floor . Here is the doorbell button . We climb the three steps  of the front steps , we cross the threshold  of the front door , and here we are at the foot of the staircase .
k.t05-01-51: The Architect. — No, this is the hall . The corridor () is at the far end. On the right, here are the drawing room () and the dining room (); opposite the dining room are the kitchen () and the pantry (); then, at the front, the study (). The veranda , with its glazed door , is next to the drawing room.
k.t05-01-52: Now we shall go up the stairs. Hold on to the handrail  and count the steps. There are fourteen. Here is the landing (): we are on the first floor .
k.t05-01-53: Opposite the stairs are the lavatory  and the dressing room (). On the right, a fine bedroom () with two windows on the front  of the house. On the left are the bathroom  and the guest room () with a large alcove (). Next to the bedroom is the children’s room (). It opens on to a wide terrace . Under this terrace is another lavatory , and against the wall, here is the bell  that is rung for dinner.
k.t05-01-54: John. — Let us go up to the second floor.
k.t05-01-55: The Architect. — There is no second floor. Under the roof there are only attic rooms  and the loft . We have finished our tour, we can go back down.
k.t05-01-56: John. — Thank you, sir, it has been most interesting. I am going to tell my father everything I have seen.
k.t06-apar-1: CHART No. 6 The Home inside, Furniture, Food, Lighting.
k.t06-apar-2: The house is finished. John’s uncle has moved into his new home, whose layout we already know. Let us now see how he has furnished it. First we shall visit:
k.t06-c1-01-1: 1. — We have come at an awkward moment, for the maid is busy cleaning the room.
k.t06-c1-02-1: 2. — On the washstand  lie, here and there, the various things one washes, combs and generally gets ready with. They are the basin  and the water jug , the hairbrush , the comb , the soap  and the sponge , and lastly a little bottle  of mouthwash.
k.t06-c1-03-1: 3. — On the floor, in front of the washstand, here is the pail  for the dirty water.
k.t06-c1-04-1: 4. — In the outer room  we can see a few coat hooks  and two umbrellas  in the umbrella stand .
k.t06-c1-05-1: 5. — On the other side of the door stands the mirrored wardrobe , which holds the linen .
k.t06-c1-06-1: 6. — Let us take advantage of the housemaid (16) making the bed  to look at its various parts. The bedstead  holds a good spring mattress , on which Justine will presently lay a woollen mattress . Then she will take from the chairs the two sheets  and the blanket . Then she will place at the head of the bed the bolster  and the pillow , which are lying with the eiderdown  on the bedside rug . She uses a feather duster on the curtains  and the canopy , and part of the work is done.
k.t06-c1-07-1: 7. — Then she will have to tidy the bedside table  a little, wind up the alarm clock , get the night light  ready, and take away the candle  to clean the candlestick.
k.t06-tit-2: The workbasket and the fireside things.
k.t06-c1-08-1: 8. — The workbasket  beside the stool  badly needs tidying too. She will have to fold up the embroidery , put away in the worktable  the thimble, the thread , the needles  and the scissors , and lock the lid of the table with the key .
k.t06-c1-09-1: 9. — On the pedestal table  in the middle, Justine will change the water in the carafe . She will put sugar in the sugar bowl , clean the sugar tongs  and take away the clothes brush .
k.t06-c1-10-1: 10. — The right-hand side of the room will give her less work, for the day bed  and its cushion  are in their proper place, and since the weather is not cold, nothing has been moved among the things belonging to the fireplace . Shovel , tongs , firedogs  and ash guard  are clean; the fire screen  has not been moved and the log box  is well stocked with firewood .
k.t06-c1-11-1: 11. — She will still have to dust the mantel clock , the candelabra  and the trinket trays , and then wipe the mirror .
k.t06-c1-12-1: 12. — As for the baby’s cradle  (the babo ), it is ready already.
k.t06-c2-01-1: 1. — Here now is the drawing room. It is a very fine room. The fireplace, in the right-hand corner, is decorated with a delicate statuette  and two handsome vases , and draped with a velvet lambrequin  .
k.t06-c2-02-1: 2. — To keep the sparks from the hearth from setting the carpet alight, a copper fire guard  has been set in front of it.
k.t06-c2-03-1: 3. — Beside it, an elegant lady’s writing desk  stands open. It is where the lady of the house  writes her letters.
k.t06-c2-04-1: 4. — The window is dressed with net curtains  held back by tiebacks  hooked to the pegs , and with heavy fabric curtains topped by a valance .
k.t06-c2-05-1: 5. — In the window recess, a jardinière  holds a green plant , a magnificent palm whose leaves reach almost as far as the oil lamp .
k.t06-c2-06-1: 6. — The lampshade  was made by Mary, the charming young lady  at the piano . Sitting very straight on the stool , she is practising a piece. She is very skilful and very tidy, as her music cabinet  shows: it is in perfect order.
k.t06-c2-07-1: 7. — Her brother Paul is looking for a book  in the bookcase . He is a boy  who is restless and quite unbearable. Hanging on to the bookcase to reach the book that is too high up, he is in danger of bringing down the bust  on top of it.
k.t06-c2-08-1: 8. — He is taking advantage, to do this silly thing, of his mother being busy talking with a friend, a lady  who has come to spend a few days with her. The mother is sitting on the sofa  beside the armchair , and her friend is on the chair , of which we can see only the back .
k.t06-c2-09-1: 9. — The big frame  hanging on the wall holds the portrait  of a relative. In the album  lying on the table are gathered the photographs  of the rest of the family. The children were leafing through it a moment ago, for the chairs  are still grouped around the table.
k.t06-c2-10-1: 10. — The porcelain Chinese vase  near the paper knife  was given to Mary on her name day, and the folding screen  that fills the corner of the room was brought back from China by her uncle.
k.t06-c2-11-1: 11. — Brightened by the handsome pictures  hanging on the wall , lit by the ceiling chandelier , whose electric lamps  shine so cheerfully in the evening, this drawing room looks very pleasant. The soft carpet  spread over the floor, and the electric bell  that is so handy, make it perfectly comfortable.
k.t06-c3-01-1: 1. — The dinner bell has rung. The whole family, except Mary, is gathered around the table. The dining room is pleasantly warmed by an excellent earthenware stove  with a slender pipe .
k.t06-c3-02-1: 2. — This room does not hold much furniture. Along the wall, above the stool , hangs a decorative little fountain . Close by is the sideboard , on which the cold dishes, the desserts and the various pieces of tableware not needed at the moment are set down.
k.t06-c3-03-1: 3. — So on the upper shelf we can see a roast chicken , a fish  and a bowl  of fruit . Below are the cheese , the bread  and the cruet stand , which holds everything needed to dress the salad: the oil, the vinegar, the salt  and the pepper . Lastly, on the bottom shelf, there is a cake  beside the mustard pot .
k.t06-c3-04-1: 4. — The dining room clock, which is called a wall clock , is a very unusual shape. It is set in a wooden frame that also holds a barometer  and a thermometer .
k.t06-c3-05-1: 5. — All round the room the walls are lined with wooden panelling  of waxed oak. A fabric door curtain  closes off well enough the door leading to the veranda. That is where the family will go to take coffee after dinner. The cups  and saucers  are already set out on the china cabinet .
k.t06-c3-06-1: 6. — Above the table a hanging lamp  is fixed to the ceiling; its very bright light fills the whole dining room in the evening.
k.t06-c3-07-1: 7. — Let us now look at the dining table  itself. When the family came in, the table was laid. On the tablecloth  there had been set, at each diner’s place, a plate , a napkin , a spoon , a fork , a knife  and a glass . There were also bottles  for the wine and a carafe  for the water.
k.t06-c3-08-1: 8. — The servant  first brought in the soup tureen , in which some soup is still steaming. He is now serving the first course , a meat dish. Then he will hand round the ones we have already named; and finally, after the dessert, he will take advantage of his employers having gone through to the veranda to clear the table and put the dining room straight again.
k.t06-c3-08-2: Note. — The everyday words to do with food are given here only in outline. The list will be completed in the two charts “The Hotel” (no. 13) and “The Market” (no. 15).
k.t06-c4-01-1: 1. — In the kitchen, at which we glance through the half-open door, we find a picturesque muddle. In front of the hearth , where the fire  crackles, the roasting jack  is set up. A fine roast  is on the spit  and is finishing cooking.
k.t06-c4-02-1: 2. — The bellows  and the coal shovel , which have just been used, have been left on the floor, along with the logs .
k.t06-c4-03-1: 3. — The top of the mantelpiece is tidy: the lantern , the matchbox holder  with the matches  in it, the candlestick  and the chamber candlestick  with its candle  are all in their places. But the big coal scuttle , full of the coal  the cook  has just been down to the cellar to fetch, has been left in the middle of the kitchen.
k.t06-c4-04-1: 4. — The truth is that the poor woman has to hurry if lunch is to be ready on time. Just now she is at the cooking range , stirring a sauce  that must not be allowed to burn.
k.t06-c4-05-1: 5. — In the oven  a cake is baking, which she has made for the children’s tea. Above the range hang the ladle  and the skimmer .
k.t06-c4-06-1: 6. — The set of pans  hanging at the back of the room is very clean. The handsome copper saucepans , the milk jug , the strainer  and the grater  have been carefully scoured.
k.t06-c4-07-1: 7. — The salt box  stands on the small dresser beside the teapot  and the oil demijohn . The drawer  probably holds the cutlery and the kitchen knives.
k.t06-c4-08-1: 8. — The broom  and the feather duster  are in a corner. The cook has just been using the chopping block ; she has left it near the window.
k.t06-c4-09-1: 9. — A hand towel  hangs on the wall next to the funnel . In this part of the kitchen are kept the grill , the chopper  and the chopping board . Then, above the chopper, on a shelf , are pots , the stew pot  with its lid , and the cauldron . The frying pan  hangs close by.
k.t06-c4-10-1: 10. — Only the copper tap  throws a gleam into this corner. The sink , on which the big pitcher  stands, must be very convenient with its little cupboard, where the vinegar cask  with its tap , the rubbish box  and the dirty dishes  are kept.
k.t06-tit-9: Other things kept in the kitchen.
k.t06-c4-11-1: 11. — The big tub  in which the vegetables  are washed, and the cast-iron cauldron  standing on the tiled floor , probably belong in that cupboard too.
k.t06-c4-12-1: 12. — The cook is certainly not short of stoves, for here on the corner of the table is a gas ring  with water heating on it in a small saucepan. The steam  escaping from it tells us it must be boiling. This water is probably for the coffee, for here at the other end of the table are the coffee pot  and the coffee grinder .
k.t06-c4-13-1: 13. — The gas ring is connected to the gas burner  by a long rubber tube .
k.t06-c4-14-1: 14. — The daily help , who comes to assist the cook, is preparing the vegetables for dinner. When they have been peeled and washed, she will put them in the pan  until it is time to cook them.
k.t06-c5-01-1: 1. — Only one more piece of prying remains before we know the main rooms of the house: to look at the fittings of the bathroom. It will not take long, for it is not large, and we shall quickly see that the bathtub  has a good water heater , that the soap dish  is within reach of the bather’s hand, and that the towel rail  must make it easy to dry the towels .
k.t06-c5-02-1: 2. — This room has its walls covered with glazed tiles , which made it possible to install a shower  without any fear that the water splashing about while it is used might damage them. A small zinc basin  for footbaths completes the furnishings.
k.t07-apar-1: SECOND SERIES CHART No. 7
k.t07-tit-2: The village in winter.
k.t07-c1-01-1: 1. — During the New Year holidays I went with my father to Newtown, a small village where he had some business to see to.
k.t07-c1-02-1: 2. — We took the stagecoach  that runs between the town and that village; but as it was very cold, the journey in so uncomfortable a vehicle was not at all pleasant.
k.t07-c1-03-1: 3. — So we were truly glad when we saw the driver pull up his coach in the square, in front of the inn  of the White Bear. The innkeeper  was waiting for us on his doorstep, quietly smoking his pipe.
k.t07-c1-03-2: He asked us in, and I did not need to be asked twice before settling myself in front of the vine-cutting fire crackling in the hearth. Then I cared nothing for the biting north wind that made the old sign  creak and carried off in black swirls the smoke  coming out of the chimney.
k.t07-c1-04-1: 4. — It was lunchtime. Without waiting any longer, we did full justice to the plain but tasty meal that was served to us <button class="apel" data-noto="en-t07-noto-1" aria-expanded="false">(*)</button>.
k.t07-c1-05-1: 5. — After lunch I went with my father, who is an insurance agent, to call on his clients. First we visited the blacksmith , who lives next to the inn. He was busy shoeing a horse. I admired the strength of his mate, who held the horse’s hoof firmly against his leather apron while the smith fastened the shoe  with heavy hammer blows.
k.t07-c1-06-1: 6. — Then we went to the village shoemaker , old Jacob. Although he had a magnificent boot for a sign, he was making do with resoling an old pair of worn-out shoes.
k.t07-c1-06-2: The old man told us with a laugh: “In town I was a ‘shoemaker’ and I had no customers. Here I am a ‘cobbler’ and there is plenty of work.”
k.t07-c1-07-1: 7. — He talked to us about his neighbour the barber , whose customers are all dissatisfied. His razors are always chipped and his scissors never cut properly. But as he is the only barber in the village, people naturally have no choice but to have him shave them and cut their hair. He is a mean and disagreeable man besides.
k.t07-c1-08-1: 8. — Fortunately the other neighbours are not like him. The wheelwright , for instance, is a kind man, hard-working and obliging. It is a pleasure to give him a cart to mend. His work is always well finished.
k.t07-c1-09-1: 9. — Old Jacob had no complaints either about the saddler , whom he sometimes helps to sew harness when the work is pressing.
k.t07-c1-09-2: My father asked him about his family. “Everyone is well. My granddaughter is at school . Her teacher  is very pleased with her; she is a good pupil . She is not like that rascal of a son of mine; he thinks of nothing but playing. The schoolmaster  cannot get him to learn a thing.”
k.t07-c1-10-1: 10. — The old man then told us the village news. A new school was to be built, for the one in the village hall had grown far too small. That would be easy enough, since it would be enough to buy part of the miller’s garden. It would suit the poor man very well. Since the cold weather began, the millstones of the mill  had not been able to grind the wheat, the wheel  being caught in the ice  of the stream .
k.t07-c1-11-1: 11. — “Speaking of building, have you seen our new church ? It looks very picturesque under its coat of snow. The crows , who no longer recognise their old bell tower, perch sadly on the big tree in the churchyard .”
k.t07-c1-12-1: 12. — The mention of the churchyard reminded the shoemaker of the people my father had known who had died in the past year. “How many graves , my dear sir, have been added to the others under the cypress ! Death took our old notary. The whole village was at his funeral.”
k.t07-c1-13-1: 13. — “There is his successor, skating on the stream. He came in a little while ago to have me mend the strap of his skate , which had broken.”
k.t07-c1-14-1: 14. — “And there, on the bank of the stream, is the new village constable . He is a former gendarme and the terror of the village rascals. They run off the moment they catch sight of his gaiters  and his peaked cap .”
k.t07-c1-15-1: 15. — “Ah! there is old Joseph bringing a cartload of faggots  for the baker. — Quite right, said my father, I recognise his team of mules . I need a word with him, and I shall take the chance. Goodbye, old Jacob.”
k.t07-c1-16-1: 16. — Just as we were going out, the village children were leaving school and rushing on to the ice slide , at the risk of falling and breaking a limb in the tumble . One of them fetched his sledge  from the wheelwright’s, sat one of his friends in it, and set off at a run.
k.t07-c1-17-1: 17. — Others rushed to a heap of snow  near the bridge  and began pelting the snowman  they had made the day before, which they had given a hat, a pipe and a school satchel slung over its shoulder.
k.t07-c1-18-1: 18. — They cared little for the freezing wind and the cold. Most of them had not even a scarf , and to warm themselves up after the snowball  fight, a handful of piping hot chestnuts  bought from old Jacqueline, the seller, who shivers with cold under her too thin shawl , was all they needed.
k.t07-tit-6: The farmhouse in spring.
k.t07-c2-01-1: 1. — For all the pleasures of winter, it is with deep joy that we greet the return of spring.
k.t07-c2-01-2: What a cheering picture a farmyard makes in the evening, in the month of May!
k.t07-c2-02-1: 2. — On the horizon the sun  is slowly setting, flooding the countryside  with its crimson rays . The busy ploughman  is hurrying to plough his field .
k.t07-c2-02-2: With his plough  drawn by a sturdy horse , he traces the furrow  in which the sower  will scatter by the handful the seed that will yield the golden ears.
k.t07-c2-03-1: 3. — The mowers  with their scythes have cut the grass of the meadow, the haymakers have dried the hay  by turning it with pitchforks  and rakes, and here they come home.
k.t07-c2-03-2: Some walk in front of the heavy cart drawn by oxen, carrying their tools on their shoulders. Others, lazier, have settled themselves comfortably on the sweet-smelling hay.
k.t07-c2-04-1: 4. — As they pass they greet in friendly fashion the gardener , busy in the orchard  pruning the fruit trees and grafting the pear trees . The plum trees  are in blossom, and in the well-manured vegetable garden  the vegetables, cabbages and lettuces are already doing well.
k.t07-c2-04-2: On the low wall, a handsome peacock  spreads its tail to show off its magnificent feathers.
k.t07-c2-05-1: 5. — The doors of the stable  are open, and one can see the hayrack and the bedding straw  of the mare  that the groom  has just unharnessed. The foal , so comical on its long legs, follows its mother, frisking about.
k.t07-c2-06-1: 6. — Near the well  the cows  go to drink from the wooden trough  that serves them for a drinking place. The calf  takes the chance to suckle, and the ox , catching the good smell of the fodder, lows cheerfully and proudly lifts its head with its powerful horns .
k.t07-c2-07-1: 7. — Everyone is at work. The maidservant  is holding the rope  of the well. She is drawing water in a bucket  to give the animals to drink. Near the barn  a man is raking up the loose straw, and in front of the door of the farmhouse  an old spinning woman , with her spinning wheel and her distaff, spins the flax or the hemp as in days gone by.
k.t07-c2-08-1: 8. — The farmer  directs all this work and gives his men their orders. He tells them to put under cover the harrow  and the pickaxe  that have been left near the kennel  of the dog .
k.t07-c2-09-1: 9. — His shouts startle a pigeon , which flies off at full speed to the dovecote , and the hens , which hurry back into the henhouse .
k.t07-c2-10-1: 10. — In front of the sheepfold , here is the old shepherd  bringing back his flock . Holding his crook , which never leaves him any more than his faded smock  does, he leads to the fold rams , ewes , lambs , goats  and kids . His faithful dog  Argus comes last and urges on the stragglers with his barking.
k.t07-c2-11-1: 11. — All this noise and bustle does not disturb the calm of the good dairy cow , which rings its bell  while it is milked in front of the door of the cowshed .
k.t07-c2-12-1: 12. — She seems to understand that she must give her milk so that the farmer’s wife  can make butter in the churn , or the excellent cheeses  that are draining on the board laid across the tub .
k.t07-c2-13-1: 13. — The whole dairy  is kept very clean by the farmhand , who has just washed the milk cans  in the big bucket he is carrying.
k.t07-c2-14-1: 14. — In his heavy clogs he walks rather clumsily, and so puts to flight the turkey , the ducks , the drakes  and the geese , which open their beaks  wide and set up an anxious clamour.
k.t07-c2-14-2: The cockerel , more warlike, raises his red comb , shakes the feathers of his tail  and lets out a ringing “cock-a-doodle-doo”.
k.t07-c2-15-1: 15. — A mother hen  is pecking about on the dung heap  with her chicks . The piglet  runs off to its mother, the huge sow  we can see beside the pigsty.
k.t07-c2-16-1: 16. — In their hutches, the rabbits  are eagerly eating the tender grass  the farmer’s daughter brings them. Jenny is very fond of her rabbits, and every day, after fetching the fresh eggs  from the henhouse, she comes to visit her little friends.

noto.t01-noto-1: (*) For first names it is also recommended to transcribe them in their Latin form. That is the only way to avoid countless variants. Besides, how would one choose between Giovanni, Jean, Johann, Jan, Hans, John, Ivan, and so on? Are we to create a special dictionary of first names? Let us take the Latin nominative and say: Ioannes, Ioanna; Iulius, Iulia; Iakobus; Andreas; Lukas. (Complete Grammar).
noto.t02-noto-1: (*) Children’s games often have purely national names. We have named them in Ido as best we could, either by drawing on the very action that characterises them, or by adopting the national name of one country or another when it is not too misleading. For example: the barrel game (German and French) is the toad in the hole  (English), in which the players try to throw their round discs through the mouth of the metal toad that stands gaping on the pierced box (barrel). Shoulder-leap  differs from leapfrog only in this: to jump over the head, the players rest their hands on their partner’s shoulders, whereas in “leapfrog” they rest their hands only on his back. — Or again, some of the players bend over while the others vault over their backs with their hands on their shoulders; the first must take the shock without giving way, the second must jump without losing their balance (see the chart itself).
noto.t05-noto-1: (*) Balk-o = German Balken, English joist, French solive, Italian travicello, Russian balka, Spanish and Portuguese viga. A technical root not yet adopted, but proposed here to render the sense of the French word solive, which is neither a trabo (French poutre) nor a small beam. It is a squared timber that carries a floor and a ceiling.
noto.t06-noto-1: (*) Babo = a small child; English baby, French bébé, Italian bambino.
noto.t06-noto-2: (*) Lambrequino = French lambrequin, Spanish lambrequines, Portuguese lambrequins, and even German and English lambrequins — so German, English, French, Portuguese and Spanish alike.
noto.t07-noto-1: (*) For the details of a meal, see charts 6 and 13.
